newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian private pension funds appear, still small.
newsitem.headline: Russian private pension funds appear, still small.

text.p: Private pension funds are appearing in Russia as the state pension fund struggles to pay off arrears, officials said on Friday.
The Ministry of Labour and Social Development now has 257 private funds registered with it, a ministry spokeswoman said.
But their assets total only 1.8 trillion roubles (about $320 million dollars), Vasily Baruchkom, chairman of the Russian state pension fund, told Reuters.
"In reality, they haven't yet had the effect which is expected of them. Maybe they will in the future," he said.
In December the average monthly state pension was 320,700 roubles ($58). Private pension funds promise to pay out more than the state pension.
The state pension fund currently owes 18 trillion roubles to pensioners, but the government has drawn up a timetable to clear these arrears by June or July.

This envisages transfers to the fund from the federal government of 5.10 trillion roubles in each of February and March and 5.65 trillion roubles in April, First Deputy Finance Minister Vladimir Petrov told the State Duma lower house of parliament last week.

Over 1995 and 1996 the fund had to borrow 14 trillion roubles from the government but hopes to bring in 11 trillion roubles from its own debtors to help pay this off, Baruchkov told a news conference.

Baruchkom said the fund had got into arrears partly because major employers such as regional governments and companies such as carmaker AvtoVAZ and metals maker Norilsk Nickel, had not paid pension contributions for their staff.
The state pension fund introduced this week a new system of social security numbers to record and calculate individual pension accounts according to individual employee's pay.
Baruchkom said this new plan would stimulate the development of private pension funds as well as straightening out the state fund.
"It will free peoples' pay which they can then voluntarily invest in private funds, which present themselves as solid investors in the economy," he said.
Baruchkom warned that at present private pension funds are risky, making uncertain investments in a still unstable economy.
The state pension fund itself is not licensed to work like a bank or commercial entity, and so does not invest in the capital markets, he said.
But this could change once the economy stabilises and the pension fund pays off its debts, he said.
Moscow's private Interregional Pension Fund, which has been working for over three years and has about 60 clients, invests in government bonds, industry and shares.
"Of course there is risk, but isn't our life one big risk," said the company's assistant director Anatoly Kuznetsov.
"This is a growing sector, with prospects and gains for everyone. People can both significantly affect their own social situation, and contribute to the economy's health as a whole."
Apart from the private fund industry, many companies operate their own in-house pension schemes, but their investments are often closely tied to the parent company.

For instance in 1995 oil group Surgut Holding's pension fund took over management of a government stake of 40 percent of Surgut Holding in exchange for a loan of 400 billion roubles to the government and an agreement to pay off 1.03 trillion roubles of Surgut Holding debt.
The pension fund is mostly owned by Surgut Holding. It is now auctioning off the stake on terms which practically ensure that Surgut Holding itself will buy it.
